Industrial software & data · 2026-07-24

The EU Data Act Creates an Exit Right. Industrial Software Still Needs a Proof of Exit.

European cloud policy now gives customers a stronger legal route out of a data-processing service. The EU Data Act has applied since 12 September 2025. It requires providers to remove contractual, commercial, technical, and organisational obstacles to switching, disclose transition terms, support machine-readable exports, and expose open interfaces.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-07-24 · 14 min read

In brief

  • 12 September 2025 | EU cloud-switching rights entered into force.
  • 12 January 2027 | switching charges must disappear.
  • 30 days | normal statutory transition period.
  • Prototype | neutral industrial portability verification remains commercially unproven.
  • 2028–2031 | repeated external acceptance would establish a durable proof layer.

The visible milestones clear only the first gate

Official study lead image

Open source visual from European Commission

Reuse: European Commission reuse policy may apply; asset-specific rights not verified · Attribution: European Commission

Those measures address the visible parts of lock-in: notice periods, transfer fees, access to data and basic interface documentation. They do not establish that an industrial customer can reproduce the operating state of a plant, building, engineering organisation or maintenance system in a competing application.

The sharper disruption thesis is sequential. The law begins to clear the formal-exit gate. Customers then encounter a second gate: proving that asset structures, identities, permissions, calculations, alarms, histories, workflows and rollback procedures survived the move. Value changes hands only when someone other than the source provider accepts that proof.

This distinction matters because the Data Act’s export boundary is narrower than an industrial application’s operating logic. Customer data may be exportable while protected algorithms, internal models, proprietary configuration logic and trade secrets remain outside the transfer. A structured archive can preserve records without preserving the decisions produced from them.

The Commission has recognized the layered nature of the problem. Article 35 covers transport, syntactic, semantic, behavioural and policy interoperability. Its February 2026 study prepared candidates for a planned Union repository of standards and open specifications. The full study was released by the Publications Office on 4 May 2026. Yet, as of 24 July 2026, the reviewed official material had not produced a named operational repository entry for an industrial SaaS category. (Commission interoperability study)

The policy architecture is advancing. The product-level clock has not clearly started.

Industrial applications fail at meaning, not file transfer

A pump record illustrates the gap. Its meaning may depend on an asset hierarchy, engineering units, alarm limits, quality flags, maintenance rules, user roles, calculation logic and interfaces to an ERP system, historian or control network. Exporting the record does not prove that a destination platform will interpret it correctly or trigger the same workflow.

A credible portability test would therefore need more than API availability. It would reconcile object counts and histories, preserve relationships and units, compare roles and entitlements, replay representative events, test calculations and exception paths, measure revalidation labour, rehearse final cutover and demonstrate rollback.

Several existing technologies supply pieces of this architecture.

OpenAPI can describe an HTTP interface. Schemathesis can generate property-based tests from OpenAPI or GraphQL descriptions. TOSCA can model application topology and lifecycle operations. OCI specifications standardise container images, runtimes and distribution. OAuth, OpenID Connect and SAML cover parts of identity exchange.

The strongest precedents come from conformance programmes. In April 2026, the Open Container Initiative described a redesigned Distribution Specification test suite that generates edge cases, exercises push, pull, discovery and management behaviour, and produces reproducible results. Eclipse Dataspace Components has been developing a modular compatibility kit that translates normative protocol requirements into executable tests. (OCI conformance) (Eclipse EDC)

These systems prove that a technical proof layer can be built. They do not prove that industrial customers will procure one. OCI tests registries, Eclipse tests data-space protocols, and OpenAPI tests interfaces. None by itself validates an engineering workflow, plant-specific permission model or safety-related operating procedure.

The commercial state is therefore best described as prototype. Constituent tools operate in production, and providers have deployed switching processes. No named neutral end-to-end industrial portability harness, paid independent verification engagement, repeat customer or externally accepted certificate was identified by the base date.

Providers have implemented process before proof

Siemens has published Data Act switching terms for Building X. The customer identifies the service and destination, observes a notice period and ordinarily completes transition within 30 days. Siemens may declare that period technically infeasible within 14 working days and propose an alternative period of up to seven months. The customer then receives at least 30 days to retrieve data. (Siemens Building X terms)

The contract demonstrates that switching has become an operating process rather than a policy abstraction. It also shows how much control the provider retains.

Detailed technical documentation remains support-mediated. Paid fees are non-refundable, and some outstanding subscription fees may remain payable through the fixed term. A customer can gain a technical right to move while retaining a substantial economic reason not to exercise it.

Dassault Systèmes follows a similar structure for 3DEXPERIENCE and other online services. It maintains a Data Register and a switching procedure, and it explicitly warns customers that format incompatibilities and transformation delays are normal migration risks. (Dassault regulatory compliance)

That warning is unusually informative. It identifies the unresolved layer directly: the destination environment must transform exported information before it becomes operationally useful.

Google Cloud, Microsoft and AWS have also formalised exit and export workflows. Google maps legal requirements to contractual steps and publishes references for data structures and formats. Microsoft directs customers to product-level export materials. AWS offers approved off-cloud transfer support through a defined credit process.

Infrastructure providers can lower transaction costs for moving data and workloads. They cannot reconstruct the semantics of an industrial application above the infrastructure layer.

Figures are drawn from provider and customer case materials and are not like-for-like comparisons.

The critical pattern is not the final outage alone. Preparation lasted from months to years, while production cutovers were compressed into hours. That asymmetry is precisely why migration evidence could have value: a customer cannot afford to discover an incomplete export or broken permission model during a 12-, 20- or 72-hour production window.

The same cases also form the strongest counterargument. Siemens, 3M, ASKUL and IHC completed difficult migrations using vendors, hyperscalers and systems integrators. No neutral portability product was required in the disclosed projects.

A new category is therefore not technically inevitable. Existing actors may simply make their private migration factories better.

The control asset is the mapping corpus

The generic test runner is unlikely to be the most defensible control point. Open-source frameworks can generate tests, execute assertions and produce signed results. The harder asset is the evolving corpus of mappings and failure cases between product families.

That corpus includes object relationships, unit conversions, identity mappings, unsupported extensions, rate-limit behaviour, custom calculations, data-quality exceptions, release-specific defects and customer validation thresholds. It becomes more useful after every migration—provided the operator can retain and reuse it.

Systems integrators already occupy this position. They perform discovery, conversion, testing, remediation, cutover and hypercare. Source vendors hold the schema knowledge and release cadence. Destination vendors control importers and can finance conversion. Large customers can build internal pipelines using API testing, data-quality tools and CI/CD systems.

A neutral provider gains control only if evidence ownership matters more than integration convenience. A manufacturer might require a report it can retain and reuse in procurement. A destination provider might demand evidence that source omissions are not its responsibility. An auditor or regulator might reject self-attestation. An insurer might eventually price migration risk against a defined rehearsal result.

None of those acceptance mechanisms was visible in a named industrial SaaS transaction by 24 July 2026. No public tender required a neutral assessor. No insurer endorsement rewarded an independent migration test. No lender tied financing to software exit evidence.

This is the missing commercial complement.

The public-company exposure map reflects the contest rather than a settled new market. Siemens, Dassault Systèmes and SAP defend source-platform control. Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft can subsidise destination migration and capture recurring infrastructure or application revenue. IONOS, Aruba and Dynamo influence the European control-plane standards layer through SECA. Accenture, Capgemini and Infosys have the delivery capabilities to productise migration factories. SGS, Bureau Veritas and Intertek possess adjacent assurance capabilities, but no verified industrial Data Act portability offering had surfaced.

Spend can move without creating a software category

Switching-charge abolition may reallocate spending, but avoided fees do not automatically become vendor revenue.

Some budgets could move into rehearsal compute, secure transfer, integrity testing, schema conversion and operational validation. Bespoke discovery could shift toward versioned export scanners. Repeated product pairs could support maintained connectors. Signed evidence might create audit, retention or assurance services.

The near-term economics are more likely to remain services-led. Semantic mapping, cybersecurity review, plant validation and exception remediation require scarce product and customer knowledge. Even a highly automated runner may sit inside a labour-intensive engagement.

Destination-funded migration further complicates value attribution. Credits and free services are customer-acquisition costs, not a new portability market. Temporary cloud consumption may already be embedded in the destination contract. Integrator revenue may substitute for existing upgrade and migration budgets rather than expand total spending.

The principal value question is therefore who owns the workflow. If the source provider supplies the export test, the incumbent retains control. If the destination vendor funds and validates the import, control transfers to the destination ecosystem. If the customer owns the canonical data model and evidence archive, control moves toward the buyer. A neutral category forms only when an independent report becomes a required commercial object.

The strongest current outcome is bundling

The most developed response is already visible in the AVEVA–AWS collaboration announced in May 2026. It combines multi-cloud architecture, migration funding, qualified operational-technology integrators and planned marketplace distribution. (AVEVA–AWS collaboration)

This structure can improve portability while preventing a neutral layer from capturing much value. The destination ecosystem can subsidise migration because it expects recurring subscription and infrastructure revenue. The integrator can maintain private mappings. The application vendor can package validation into support or professional services.

Three outcomes remain credible through the end of the decade.

In the first, repository specifications become machine-testable, providers publish structured export manifests, and customers require rehearsals before renewal or termination. A customer-owned or independent proof layer reaches demonstration and then repeat procurement.

In the second, providers and destination ecosystems bundle exporters, validators, credits and migration services. Switching improves, but evidence remains controlled by the parties competing for the workload.

In the third, legal compliance exposes rather than removes residual lock-in. Customers retrieve structured data but still face months of semantic conversion, revalidation and contract exposure. Systems integrators gain work while source vendors preserve attachment through complexity.

The evidence currently favours the second and third outcomes over the first.

The historical base rate argues for a narrow thesis

The closest policy precedent is the EU’s earlier cloud-switching work. A 2018 Commission study documented barriers involving data, applications, contracts and interoperability. Voluntary and contractual measures did not remove them, contributing to binding legislation years later.

The similarity is persistence: interface documentation and contractual rights alone did not make application switching routine. The difference is that the Data Act now creates enforceable duties and a mechanism for listing standards and open specifications.

Technical conformance programmes offer a more positive precedent. OCI and Kubernetes show that normative requirements can become executable tests and support multi-vendor ecosystems. Mobile number portability shows that a legal right becomes operational when the transferred object and process are tightly bounded.

Industrial SaaS is less tractable. A phone number, container image or Kubernetes API exposes a more standardised object than a configured engineering or operations platform. TOSCA and earlier cloud-portability initiatives also show that mature standards can coexist with limited application-level switching.

The thesis that survives is therefore narrower: the Data Act creates a real proof problem, but it does not guarantee a neutral proof market.

What to watch

  • By 31 July 2027, an EU publication names an Article 35 specification, version and service scope.
  • Within 18 months of that listing, an industrial provider publishes a machine-readable export manifest.
  • By 31 December 2029, a named cross-provider switch reports downtime and revalidation effort.
  • By 31 December 2030, an industrial tender requires quantified rehearsal or rollback criteria.
  • By 31 December 2031, one neutral evidence profile is accepted in two independent migrations.

The decisive event is repeated external acceptance. A test profile used internally by one integrator remains a project tool. The same profile accepted by two customers and relied on by a destination, auditor, regulator or insurer becomes infrastructure.

Until that happens, industrial portability will advance mainly through provider compliance, destination-funded migration and systems-integration work. The Data Act has created the right to leave. The commercial contest is over who gets to certify that the operating system actually arrived.
